data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The nocturnal UHI is primarily a release of stored sensible heat. Urban materials (concrete, asphalt, brick) have high thermal mass and heat capacity, so they sequester daytime solar energy and release it slowly after sunset. The single best cross-city predictor is the total thermal mass / impervious surface area of the built fabric: cities with more masonry and asphalt per unit area store more daytime heat and release it over a longer nocturnal period, yielding a larger night-time temperature surplus.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If both urban and rural substrates have similar heat capacities and thermal masses (e.g., a city built on bedrock with thin paving), the differential storage release vanishes.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If daytime cloud cover prevents significant solar absorption, there is no stored heat to release at night and the mechanism collapses.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If highly conductive substrate or subsurface drainage removes heat faster than it can radiate outward, the storage-release pathway is undermined.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Impervious, high-heat-capacity urban surfaces absorb solar radiation during the day and store it as sensible heat in their thermal mass. After sunset, the rural countryside\u2014with lower heat capacity and less thermal mass\u2014cools rapidly. The city's masonry and asphalt continue to release stored heat into the near-surface air throughout the night. The magnitude of this effect scales with the total impervious surface area and thermal mass of the city: more dense, massive construction means more daytime storage and a slower nocturnal cooling rate, hence a larger UHI.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
